facts.title: A spark between two fingers
facts.body: Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam (c. 1512) on the Sistine ceiling freezes the instant before life jumps the gap — God and Adam almost touch.

facts.title: Adam waiting to wake
facts.body: Adam reclines on bare ground, body already classical and complete, waiting for the charge that will make him live.

facts.title: God in a rush of angels
facts.body: God surges forward wrapped in a wind-blown mantle, carried by angels — energy against Adam’s stillness.

facts.title: The most famous nearly-touch
facts.body: The gap between the two index fingers is the painting’s voltage — creation as a held breath.

facts.title: A face under the arm
facts.body: A feminine face looks out from under God’s arm — often read as Eve waiting her turn, or the yet-unborn human soul.

facts.title: A cluster of spirits
facts.body: Wingless putti brace and lean inside the mantle, turning God’s arrival into a living cloud.

facts.title: Unfinished ground
facts.body: Adam’s side of the fresco is spare rock and slope — a world not yet green.

facts.title: A mantle like a brain — or a sail
facts.body: God’s cloak billows into a shape some viewers compare to a human brain; others see pure storm and motion.
